claims.claim: A sugar-cube-sized amount of neutron-star material would weigh about 1 billion tons (about 10^12 kg) on Earth
claims.definition: NASA's standard public analogy: neutron-star interior density (~10^17-10^18 kg/m3) applied to a ~1 cm3 cube
claims.measured_value: ~1 billion tons per sugar cube (~10^12 kg)
claims.authoritative_source: NASA Science - Neutron Stars; NASA Imagine the Universe!
claims.notes: The popular 'weighs as much as Mount Everest' variant fails arithmetic: Everest is ~10^14-10^15 kg, i.e. 100-1000x heavier. This story uses the computed pyramid comparison instead (see pyramids_170_computed).

claims.claim: When a giant star's fuel ends, the core collapses in seconds; protons and electrons are crushed together into neutrons
claims.definition: Core collapse of a massive star (at least ~8 solar masses); neutronization via electron capture during the collapse
claims.authoritative_source: NASA Science - Neutron Stars; NASA/ESA supernova pages

claims.claim: A neutron star packs roughly 1.4 times the Sun's mass into a sphere about 20 kilometers wide
claims.definition: Canonical neutron-star parameters: mass ~1.4 solar masses (the Chandrasekhar-forming core), diameter ~20 km
claims.authoritative_source: NASA Science - Neutron Stars; NASA Imagine the Universe!
claims.notes: Known population spans ~1.17-2.35 solar masses; 1.4 is the canonical textbook value. Narration uses the exact figure.

claims.claim: 1 billion tons is roughly the combined mass of 170 Great Pyramids of Giza
claims.definition: Computed comparison: Great Pyramid mass ~5.9 million tonnes; 10^9 t / 5.9x10^6 t = 169.5, rounded to 170
claims.authoritative_source: Computed from Great Pyramid mass estimates (~5.9 Mt) plus the NASA sugar-cube figure
claims.notes: Explicitly a computed comparison, not a measured record. Chosen over the popular Everest analogy, which fails arithmetic by 2-3 orders of magnitude.

claims.claim: A fragment dropped on Earth would punch straight through the ground
claims.definition: Physics illustration: density ~10^17 kg/m3 vs crust ~3x10^3 kg/m3 - no known material offers meaningful resistance; the fragment falls through the planet
claims.authoritative_source: Physics estimate from NASA density figures (standard back-of-envelope published widely in popular science)
claims.notes: Illustrative physics statement, marked as such. The narration phrase 'like the crust was paper' is simile, not a measured claim.

claims.claim: Neutron stars were first detected in 1967: a radio telescope caught a pulsar flashing every 1.3 seconds, initially nicknamed LGM-1 (Little Green Men)
claims.definition: 'only found' in the narration means first observational detection: PSR B1919+21 (CP 1919), discovered by Jocelyn Bell Burnell under Antony Hewish, period 1.3373 s, briefly nicknamed LGM-1
claims.authoritative_source: Hewish, Bell et al., Nature 217, 709-713 (1968); NASA/JPL pulsar history
claims.notes: Narration 'every 1.3 seconds' rounds 1.3373 s. The nickname LGM-1 ('Little Green Men') is historical fact.

claims.claim: The nearest known neutron star is about 400 light-years away; Voyager 1 would need about 7 million years to cover that distance
claims.definition: RX J1856.5-3754, closest known isolated neutron star, distance ~120 pc ~ 400 ly (HST parallax); Voyager 1 speed ~17 km/s ~ 3.6 AU/yr, so 400 ly ~ 25.3 million AU ~ 7 million years
claims.current_record_holder: RX J1856.5-3754 (closest known; nearer unconfirmed candidates may exist)
claims.measured_value: ~400 ly (~120 pc); ~7 million years at Voyager 1 speed (computed)
claims.authoritative_source: HST parallax (Walter & Lattimer 2002, ApJ 576, L145); Voyager 1 mission status (NASA)
claims.notes: 'nearest known' is the defensible form: unconfirmed candidates may exist. The Voyager travel time is a computed illustration.
claims.recheck_note: V5 §18: nearest-known-neutron-star rankings change (RX J1856.5-3754 parallax revisions; Calvera candidate). Re-verify against current literature before any reuse — not evergreen.
